newsitem.title: USA: U.S. YIELD CURVE - 10-yr TIPS still surprising mkt.
newsitem.headline: U.S. YIELD CURVE - 10-yr TIPS still surprising mkt.

text.p: It has only been about two weeks since the U.S. Treasury sold index-linked bonds for the first time, but in that period, the 10-year notes have performed better than most on Wall Street had predicted.
In fact, the Treasury Inflation Protected Securities, known in the market by the acronym TIPS, have outperformed their regular 10-year note counterpart.

Since their auction on January 29, the TIPS's yield has fallen from about 3.45 percent to 3.29 percent -- a 16 basis point decline. Meanwhile, regular 10-year notes, at 6.62 percent on January 29, were 20 basis points lower at 6.42 percent. Throw in the February 2007 10-year notes sold on Wednesday, and the decline is 23 basis points.

"We had expected (TIPS) to move about half as much as 10-year yields," wrote J.P. Morgan & Co Inc's Treasury market strategist Nanette Abuhoff in her weekly commentary on Monday. TIPS "have outperformed because of strong demand from investors as well as dealers. The recent slew of corporate issuance means (TIPS) are likely to hold their scarcity value," she added.
Market participants, however, were quick to point out that comparing the 10-year TIPS to regular 10-year notes is like comparing apples and oranges.

"You can't trade them against 10-year notes," said Scott Graham, a 10-year trader at Prudential Securties Inc. "People haven't yet figured out the proper hedge. They are not a trading vehicle; they are an investment vehicle."

One head trader at a leading primary dealership noted that liquidity in the TIPS is just a fraction of regular 10-year note trading. Indeed, on Wednesday, trading volume, according to GovPX was $26 million in 10-year TIPS, while the when-issued 10-year note garnered $2.15 billion and the outstanding 10-year note, $3.98 billion.

"They are still in a cloud as to what they are worth," the head trader said, noting that the 10-year TIPS trade more like a note with a duration of three to seven years. "I would like to see how they trade if the market goes down 70 points."
Traders said retail interest was still low, while STRIP demand was also weak. Some said that derivatives players were looking at TIPS' value.

Prior to the index-linked bond auction, sentiment over TIPS was bearish, and even minutes before the bidding deadline, traders figured demand would be weak and the notes would price at a rate of 3.50 percent or higher.
The Street, though, was stunned when they priced at 3.449 percent. Since then, short-covering pushed the notes to 3.24 percent, before moving back up near 3.30 percent on Wednesday.

"No one wants nominal yields below 3.25 percent" if there is no change in inflation expectations, Graham said. "At 3.20, they will hit a wall, but when they go up to 3.50, 3.60, they will have a bid that won't go away."
And since TIPS will likely underperform in a "down" market and do well in an "up" market, the spread between 10-year TIPS and regular 10-year notes will be volatile, he added.

"I don't interpret the (TIPS') recent behavior as surprising," said John Youngdahl, money market economist at Goldman, Sachs & Co Inc. "It's still early. They only settled in early February, so they have only been around for all of a week."
